Pneumococal vacccination during early infancy results in significantly lower incidence of AOM due to Streptococcus pneumoniae but not all-cause AOM. Pneumococal vacccination is uniformly recommended by federal and state governments and by medical organizations. A

background.definition: Acute otitis media (AOM) is characterized by the rapid onset of signs and symptoms of an acute infection accompanied with middle ear effusion, and inflammation of the tympanic membrane.

list.listitem: Sixty two visits per 100 persons per year for children younger than 1 year; 16.5 per 100 persons per year for children between the ages of 1 and 12 years.
Approximately 23% of children in the United States have had an episode of AOM by the age of 1 year, increasing to about 60% by 3 years of age.
Associated cost of AOM in 2017 was approximately $4 billion USD.
AOM is usually a sequelae of an acute viral upper respiratory infection.
Middle ear fluid is sterile in one-third of patients meeting diagnostic criteria.

Bacteria commonly cultured from middle ear aspirates include Streptococcus pneumoniae (30%), Haemophilus influenzae (25%), Moraxella catarrhalis (10%), Group A Streptococcus and Staphylococcus aureus (10%), and multiple pathogens (5%).

A systematic review of 19 studies conducted in the post-PCV era showed that Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae are the 2 predominant bacteria. There has been no clear change in antimicrobial resistance of Streptococcus pneumonia observed.
Children younger than 2 years treated with amoxicillin for AOM are more likely to develop a subsequent episode of AOM over the next 3 years than children who were not treated (NNT = 5).
Pacifier use is associated with a small increase in the likelihood of recurrent AOM.
Acute upper respiratory infections, allergies, and exposure to particulates, including cigarette smoke, can cause swelling of the eustachian tube.
The eustachian tube swelling can cause negative middle ear pressure and accumulation of serous fluid. The fluid may become infected with viruses or bacteria.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Treatment in children less than 2 years old as compared with no treatment

list.listitem: Prevention of AOM is directed at risk factor reduction, including encouraging breast feeding, eliminating pacifier use, eliminating environmental smoke exposure, eliminating exclusive supine feedings in infants, and decreasing day-care exposure. C
Influenza vaccine may provide a modest reduction in the rate of AOM. B

Pneumococal vacccination during early infancy results in significantly lower incidence of AOM due to Streptococcus pneumoniae (moderate- to high-certainty evidence) but not all-cause AOM (low- to moderate-certainty evidence). It is uniformly recommended by federal and state governments and by medical organizations. A

Probiotics may decrease the incidence of AOM in children with normal risks to the disease (moderate-certainty evidence) but do not appear beneficial for at-risk children (high-certainty evidence). This discrepancy warrants careful interpretation and generalization. The best strain, frequency, timing and length of administration have yet to be determined. B

Long-term (≥ 6 weeks) antibiotic therapy, given once or twice a day, may decrease recurrent AOM in at-risk children from 3 to 1.5 episodes per year. However, given this modest benefit, the potential for increasing antibiotic resistance, and cessation of benefit after stopping antibiotics, long-term AOM prophylaxis with antibiotics is not recommended. B
Diagnose acute otitis media (AOM) in patients presenting with moderate to severe bulging of the tympanic membrane (TM) or new onset of otorrhea not due to otitis externa. B
AOM can be diagnosed in children presenting with mild bulging of the TM and less than 48 hours of ear pain (ear tugging, holding, or rubbing in a nonverbal child) or intense erythema of the TM. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Ear canal erythema, swelling, and tenderness on otoscopic exam
Mastoid process erythema, tenderness, typically high fever, and irritability
Presence of middle ear fluid that either is asymptomatic or lacks signs of inflammation
Vessicles typically seen on the tympanic membrane
Ear canal obstructed by cerumen, which can cause pain and decreased hearing

list.listitem: The clinical diagnosis of AOM can be made based on the presence of all of the following: (1) acute onset of fever or signs of ear pain, (2) middle ear fluid as demonstrated by exam or diagnostic testing, and (3) signs of middle ear inflammation including erythema or purulent middle ear fluid.

Consider AOM in a child presenting with acute onset of ear pain, ear rubbing, parental suspicion, and excessive crying. In children with suspected AOM, these are the symptoms that best increase the likelihood of AOM, while absence of URI, absence of parental suspicion, and absence of otalgia best rule it out.

However, a Finnish study of 469 children between the ages of 6 and 35 months in whose parents suspected AOM found that no sign, symptom, or cluster of signs or symptoms reliably differentiated AOM from an upper respiratory infection.

The diagnosis of AOM is supported by the presence of middle ear effusion seen on otoscopy or by decreased tympanic membrane mobility on pneumatic otoscopy. The diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of middle ear inflammation.
Specific physical exam findings that best rule in AOM include bulging TM, distinctly impaired mobility, and cloudy or distinctly red TM.

Children under 10 years of age with fever (>37.5 C) or vomiting may benefit from immediate antibiotic therapy in the short-term (day 3). However, those without fever or vomiting do not appear to beneft from antibiotics and have comparable short-term outcomes to children without fever or vomiting treated immediately with antibiotics.
Laboratory and radiological tests are not needed for the diagnosis of AOM.
If available, typanometry or acoustic reflectometry can aid in the detection of middle ear fluid but do not replace otoscopy for the determination of inflammation.
Digital otoscopy can improve agreement between the conclusions of trainees and their supervisors.

Ariticial intelligence (AI) decision-support tool to evaluate mobile-device captured otoscopic videos may improve the diagnosis of acute otitis media in children, with a 93.8% sensitivity and 93.5% specificity. However, this new technique was not compared to pneumatic otoscopy, and length of time to diagnosis was not reported. Parents appear receptive to this new technology.
See chapter on otitis media (chronic serous).
Consider AOM in a child presenting with acute onset of ear pain, ear rubbing, parental suspicion, or excessive crying.
Diagnosis of AOM is supported by presence of middle ear effusion and middle ear inflammation on otoscopy.
See for a suggested approach to treatment.
Recommend either acetaminophen or ibuprofen for short-term pain relief in children 6 months to 16 years of age with AOM, based on low quality evidence from systematic review. B

National guidelines recommend oral analgesics alone (without the use of antibiotics) for children older than 2 years without signs of severe illness (moderate to severe otalgia or fever equal to or higher than 39°C) and if short-term follow-up is available. B
A delayed prescription approach produces equivalent results, reduces antibiotic use, and improves parent's satisfaction, when compared to immediate treatment. A

If antibiotic treatment is chosen, amoxicillin at a dosage of 80 to 90 mg/kg/day divided twice daily for 5 to 10 days is the recommended first-line antibiotic by US guidelines. Some European guidelines recommend 30 to 60 mg/kg/day. B
Antihistamines, decongestants, topical analgesic ear drops, intranasal corticosteroids, intranasal surfactant, adenoidectomy, and adenotonsillectomy are not effective for treating AOM. B

A Cochrane review evaluating 13 studies involving 3401 children found that antibiotics do not reduce pain at 24 hours or at 4-7 days, but may reduce pain slightly at days 2-3 (NNTB = 20). This must be balanced against adverse events like diarrhea, vomiting, and rash caused by antibiotics (NNTH = 14). Modest benefits were seen in children with tympanic perforations, contralateral AOM, and abnormal tympanometry at 2-4 weeks. The authors concluded that in high-income countries where AOM usually resolves without complications, expectant management may be a reasonable approach, with the focus on pain management and with antibiotics taking a limited role.
A secondary analysis of an RCT of amoxicillin-clavulanate vs. placebo suggested that children with severe bulging of the tympanic membrane are most likely to benefit from antibiotics (NNT = 2).
See for a suggested approach to antibiotic treatment of AOM.
If there is no symptomatic improvement after 72 hours or if symptoms worsen, initiate antibiotic treatment with amoxicillin. Antibiotic treatment does not prevent middle ear effusion.

If antibiotic treatment is chosen, US guidelines recommend amoxicillin at a dosage of 80 to 90 mg/kg/day divided twice daily for 5 to 10 days is the recommended first-line antibiotic. Five days of treatment is equivalent to a 10-day course. Azithromycin can be used for amoxicillin allergy (30 mg/kg as a single dose) or in patients with persistent or recurrent AOM (20 mg/kg daily for 3 days).Consider beginning therapy with amoxicillin/clavulanate in children presenting with severe otalgia or temperature ≥39°C.

A review of 15 European guidelines found that most recommend a watchful waiting approach, and if antibiotics are chosen recommend 5 to 7 days of amoxicillin, some recommending 75 to 90 mg/kg/day and others 30 to 60 mg/kg/day.

A Cochrane review concluded that once daily or twice daily amoxicillin dosing, with or without clavulanate, appears comparable to administering amoxicillin threes times a day for children 12 years of age or younger with AOM, based on low quality evidence from 5 RCTs involving 1601 children.

If no symptomatic improvement occurs after 72 hours, switch to amoxicillin/clavulanate 90 mg/kg/day (of amoxicillin component) divided twice daily for 10 days or intramuscular ceftriaxone for 3 days. A 5-day course of amoxicillin/clavulanate is less effective at resolving symptoms than a 10-day course, and does not reduce the incidence of diarrhea or diaper dermatitis.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies with 5600 children aged 6 months to 15 years found that efficacy of azithromycin is comparable to amoxicillin/ clavulanate as well as being better tolerated by children.

A meta-analysis of 82 studies of antibiotic treatment of AOM in children found that diarrhea and generalized rash occur most frequently with amoxicillin-clavulanate and high-dose amoxicillin, and less commonly with azithromycin.

A Dutch open randomized controlled non-inferiority trial of 58 children compared topical antibiotic-corticosteroid eardrops to usual oral antibiotics in children with AOM and otorrhea. The study was terminated early and non-inferiority of eardrops vs. oral antibiotics could not be determined. In this small sample size those assigned to the eardrops had lower resolution of ear pain, fever, and ear discharge compared to those receiving oral antibiotics.

Parents' expectation of antibiotic prescription for AOM are not as frequent as clinicians think. Presenting information about the pros and cons of antibiotic use and letting parents decide whether and when to start treatment increases their satisfaction with the visit and may decrease antibiotic use.Watchful waiting is a recommended option for children between the ages of 6 and 24 months with an uncertain diagnosis and for all children older than 2 years, unless severe otalgia or high fever (≥39°C) is present. Most children will have resolution of symptoms within 3 days. A delayed prescription approach involves giving a prescription and asking parents to wait 2 to 3 days before starting therapy, or asking parents to call for a prescription in 2 to 3 days if symptoms don't resolve. This approach does not increase the risk of mastoiditis.

An RCT showed providing training on best practices and communications regarding antibiotics stewardship and individualized antibiotic prescribing feedback reports decreased antibiotic prescribing for acute respiratory tract infections including AOM. However, a cluster randomized trial involving 27 Australian general practices with 122 general practitioners (GPs) found no difference between GPs who received brief shared decision-making intervention (video-delivered training) and control group in terms of antibiotic prescription for acute respiratory infections (AOM, sore throat, acute bronchitis), even if the intervention group demonstrated improved knowledge.
Despite widely available treatment guidelines, the utilization of broad-spectrum antibiotics and longer than recommended treatment duration is still common.

For children 6 months to 16 years of age, monotherapy with either acetaminophen or ibuprofen appears better than placebo in the short-term (48 hours), based on low quality evidence. There is no evidence of superiority of either medication, and there is uncertainty whether combination therapy is better than monotherapy with either medication.

Provide pain control with acetaminophen (paracetamol) for children older than 2 years without signs of severe illness if short-term follow-up is available. Antibiotics are generally not needed for this group. There is insufficient evidence to know whether analgesic ear drops are effective.

However, a Dutch cluster randomized trial with 37 general practices and 224 children with AOM compared a training program encouraging discussion of pain management and use of acetaminophen and/or ibuprofen with usual care. It found no difference in symptoms but more use of analgesics in the intervention group.
If AOM is accompanied by rupture of the TM, topical antibiotic ear drops can be used instead of systemic antibiotics.

An RCT showed a clinically important reduction in AOM symptoms in children of parents shown video discharge instructions for the identification and treatment of pain and fever in AOM as compared to the children of parents given discharge instructions via paper handout. This video can be found at https://vimeo.com/334292365.

Decongestants and antihistamines, or their combination, do not relieve symptoms or hasten resolution of AOM. Intranasal steroid use in children with purulent rhinitis or an upper respiratory infection does not decrease and may increase AOM.
Intranasal corticosteroids do not appear to relieve signs of Eustachian tube dysfunction compared to placebo, based on a systematic review of 8 RCTs.
Intranasal surfactant does not improve clinical outcomes in young children with AOM.
Based on very low- to low-quality evidence, a Cochrane review found uncertain evidence for the effectiveness of systemic corticosteroids for children with AOM.

Myringotomy and tympanostomy may be useful in decreasing recurrence of AOM in children with frequent recurrences, generally 3 or more episodes in 6 months or 4 or more episodes over the course of a year.
Adenoidectomy and adenotonsillectomy offer minimal benefit in children with recurrent AOM. Tympanostomy does not affect language acquisition or development.

A randomized clinical trial of 250 children ages 6 months to 35 months with recurrent otitis media showed no significant difference in the rates of acute otitis media during a 2 year period when comparing tympanostomy tube placement with medical management.
Giving xylitol-containing gum or syrup 5 times daily to healthy children in day care decreases their likelihood of AOM.
A naturopathic ear drop may be effective in decreasing AOM symptoms.
There is conflicting evidence regarding the effect of zinc supplements on preventing future episodes of AOM.
Children should be hospitalized and otolaryngology consultation obtained if mastoiditis or spread of the infection to the surrounding structures is suspected.

In research populations, 37% of untreated children will have pain and/or fever after 3 to 7 days. Over half (55%) of children less than 2 years old who are untreated will have pain and/or fever after 3 to 7 days, and 25% of children 2 years old or older will still have symptoms after 3 to 7 days. B
Symptom resolution rate is similar (60%) with or without treatment 24 hours after diagnosis and after 2 to 3 days (90%). C
Children younger than 2 years will have symptoms for a median of 8 days. B

For children with otitis media, one episode of mastoiditis is prevented for every 4831 children who are treated. The incidence of acute mastoiditis in children in the U.S. was stable from 1997 through 2006, at 1.6 to 1.9 per 100,000 person-years. Most children who develop mastoiditis will not have had otitis media diagnosed in the previous 3 months. B

Strong predictors of recurrent AOM include age at first AOM and daycare attendance. Among children with recurrent AOM, 83% of recurrence occurs within 6 months and 97% within 10 months of initial episode, otherwise known as the window of susceptibility. Tympanostomy tubes may be relatively ineffective since most of them are placed outside this window. B

The observation without antibiotic option may require significant effort on the part of clinicians to train parents who expect antibiotic treatment, but shared decision making with an optional antibiotic prescription improves parent satisfaction.Only 38% of the prescriptions were filled compared with 87% in directed antibiotic treatment groups.
Regardless of antibiotic treatment, some children will have fever, ear pain, or both, for several days.
Antibiotic therapy can often be delayed for 2 to 3 days and started only in children who continue to have pain or fever.
Appropriate doses of acetaminophen (paracetamol) or ibuprofen will decrease symptoms.
Febrile infants 0 to 8 weeks of age should undergo full sepsis workup as atypical pathogens such as group B Streptococcus, gram-negative enteric bacteria, and Chlamydia trachomatis can be involved.

cell.label: Acute otitis media. Any of following: severe infection (moderate to severe otalgia or temperature ≥39°C), immunocompromise, or sepsis; age <6 months; or age 6-24 months with certain diagnosis of AOM?
Option of analgesics and watchful waiting. Symptoms resolve or improve at 48-72 hours?
Follow-up as needed to ensure resolution of episode. Symptoms recur?
Amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/day (macrolide if allergic); if severe otalgia or fever give amoxicillin/ clavulanate 90 mg/kg/day (ceftriaxone IM if allergic). Symptoms resolve or improve at 48-72 hours?
Switch to amoxicillin/clavulanate 90 mg/kg/day for 10 days if initially amoxicillin, or ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg/day for 3 days if initially amoxicillin/clavulanate. Symptoms resolve?
Consider tympanocentesis with culture; change in antibiotics to clindamycin; and/or imaging if complications suspected.
